title: India Reportedly Sets Two Conditions for Sheikh Hasina's Return to Bangladesh
excerpt: A BBC Bangla report says New Delhi wants a Bangladesh Army-led transfer and a guaranteed appeal with a fresh trial; India's foreign ministry declined to comment.
body:
• India has reportedly set two conditions for Sheikh Hasina's return to Bangladesh, according to a BBC Bangla report: the Bangladesh Army must take responsibility for bringing her back, and Dhaka must guarantee she can appeal her death sentence and face a fresh trial.
  • MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal declined to comment on the report on November 13, saying only that the legal-matter remark referred to the extradition part of the case.
  • Hasina, who fled to India on August 5, 2024, has said she intends to return in December 2026 and applied for a fresh passport on November 9, but Indian officials reportedly doubt Dhaka will facilitate a December return.
  • Neither government has officially confirmed the reported discussions, so the conditions remain a report, not an announced agreement.

India is reportedly seeking two guarantees before it facilitates the return of former Bangladesh prime minister Sheikh Hasina from exile in New Delhi, according to a BBC Bangla report summarised by The Business Standard. The report, published on Thursday and citing unnamed Indian government and military officials, says New Delhi has been working for several months on a viable path for Hasina's return, and has outlined the conditions as her continued stay becomes, in the report's telling, increasingly uncomfortable for India diplomatically.

The two reported conditions

The first condition concerns the transfer itself. India reportedly wants Bangladesh's military to take responsibility for bringing Hasina home, preferably aboard a Bangladeshi military aircraft — mirroring how she arrived in India on August 5, 2024. As an alternative, Bangladeshi military personnel could receive her at a designated point along the land border, with India prepared to provide transport and logistical support, the report said. The report also said India wants assurances that the Bangladesh Army will protect her safety after she returns, and that Indian officials do not want to hand her over to a Bangladeshi aircraft as a prisoner, because that could send a negative message to political allies in neighbouring countries including Nepal, Sri Lanka and the Maldives.

The second condition concerns the courts. New Delhi reportedly wants Dhaka to guarantee that Hasina can appeal against the death sentence imposed over the July 2024 uprising and killings, and that she will face a fresh trial. The Business Standard and Madhyamam's report of the same BBC Bangla account both say India wants the proceedings held under international scrutiny.

"We can never knowingly push her towards the gallows. Rather, we want her to have an opportunity for a fresh, impartial and fair trial."

— Unnamed senior Indian foreign ministry official, quoted by BBC Bangla

What India said on the record

India has not confirmed any of this publicly. Asked on November 13 about reports that India wanted a military aircraft and fair-trial assurances, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal declined to comment. "When I talked about the legal matter, it is about the extradition part of it. To the other part of your question, I have no comment to offer," he said at a media briefing in New Delhi, according to The Business Standard. That distinction matters: New Delhi's on-record position remains that Dhaka's extradition request — first sent by diplomatic letter in December 2024, with several follow-ups since, and neither accepted nor rejected so far — is a legal matter to be dealt with accordingly. The reported return arrangement sits outside that public position, and Bangladesh's government has also not officially confirmed or responded to the BBC Bangla report.

Why the December plan looks uncertain

Hasina has maintained that she intends to return in December 2026, and on November 9 she applied for a fresh passport — her first official contact with Dhaka since going into exile, according to Madhyamam. Yet the BBC Bangla report said Indian officials doubt whether Dhaka genuinely wants her back now, pointing to an energy crisis, garment workers' protests, and the risk that her return could intensify political instability. It said it remained uncertain where she would be on December 31, 2026.

The report also said India had initially explored sending Hasina to a third country without success, and now views a return followed by participation in Bangladesh's judicial process as the most practical option. It pointed to regular military-to-military contact, including weekly conversations that former Indian Army chief General Manoj Pande has said he held with Bangladesh Army chief General Waker-Uz-Zaman after July 2024.

What to watch

For now, treat the two conditions as a reported position, not a deal. The tests are concrete: whether Dhaka accepts an army-led transfer and an appeal with a fresh trial, and whether a December date is actually announced. In the same briefing, Jaiswal reiterated that India desires a positive, constructive and forward-looking relationship with Bangladesh — a reminder that both capitals are keeping the wider relationship running while the Hasina question remains unresolved.
